summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would make several technical updates to the Customs Act 1901.
It would allow the customs agency to authorise future job roles, extend controls to arrival points, and improve reporting and application processes.
Customs powers would be expanded to cover baggage and cargo of domestic passengers on international flights and voyages.
changes: The bill would let authorisations cover positions created after the authorisation is given.
It would extend customs controls to places where ships and aircraft arrive under section 58 of the Act.
It would provide more flexibility for reporting ship and aircraft arrivals and reporting stores and prohibited goods.
It would improve application processes for several permissions and support online applications.
It would extend customs examination powers to domestic passenger baggage and domestic cargo on international flights or voyages.
It would improve how the infringement notice scheme interacts with the claims process for prohibited imports.
summary.affected: The Australian Customs and Border Protection Service and people or entities involved in international flights and voyages.

speeches.speaker: Scott Morrison
speeches.brief: Introduced the Customs Amendment Bill 2014, extending Customs examination powers to domestic travellers' baggage and domestic cargo on international flights and voyages, and to non-proclaimed arrival points such as cruise ship stops and offshore installations, to close border-risk gaps exploited by criminal entities.

speeches.speaker: Matt Thistlethwaite
speeches.brief: Supported the Customs Amendment Bill, said Australian cruise ship passenger numbers hit a record 833,000 in 2013 with 20 per cent growth outpacing any other market, and explained the bill would let a person make a claim for seized goods up to 30 days after an infringement notice is withdrawn.

speeches.speaker: Steve Irons
speeches.brief: Supported the Customs Amendment Bill, reported that Perth Customs officers seized over 12 kilograms of methamphetamine and more than 2,000 prohibited weapons from air cargo between January and October, and said the government committed $88 million in additional funding for customs screening plus a further $480.5 million over four years for Australia's Strategic Border Command.

speeches.speaker: Justine Elliot
speeches.brief: Supported the Customs Amendment Bill as a former police officer, explaining it would extend Customs' examination powers to domestic travellers' bags and cargo on international flights, and said reports on ship arrivals must currently be made within 24 hours while aircraft reports are required within three hours.

speeches.speaker: Nickolas Varvaris
speeches.brief: Supported the Customs Amendment Bill, said air cargo inspection rates fell from 60 per cent under the Howard government to less than 5 per cent under Labor, and cited the 2012 seizure of 220 Glock pistols by New South Wales Police rather than Customs as evidence of the previous government's cuts of 700 customs jobs and $734.8 million in funding.

speeches.speaker: Dennis Jensen
speeches.brief: Supported the Customs Amendment Bill, said it would close loopholes allowing goods to be exchanged between domestic and international travellers, and noted the new Australian Border Force is due to commence on 1 July 2015.

speeches.speaker: David Coleman
speeches.brief: Criticized Labor's record on customs and border protection, citing air cargo inspections falling from 60 per cent under the Howard government to 5 per cent under Labor, and commended the Customs Amendment Bill 2014 for extending inspection powers to non-proclaimed places and to domestic legs of international flights.

speeches.speaker: Don Randall
speeches.brief: Detailed six technical changes in the Customs Amendment Bill including extending customs control to non-proclaimed places and to domestic legs of international flights, blamed Labor for cutting Customs' workforce and cargo screening funding, and outlined a $480 million government package to fund the incoming Australian Border Force.

speeches.speaker: Ian Goodenough
speeches.brief: Explained that the Customs Amendment Bill would extend Customs powers to examine domestic goods on domestic legs of international flights and goods landed at non-proclaimed places, and argued Australia's vast coastline made stronger border monitoring necessary.

speeches.speaker: Ewen Jones
speeches.brief: Described difficulty securing customs, immigration and quarantine services for a proposed new international flight from Townsville to Bali due to high on-ground costs, thanked the minister for his assistance, and argued Australia must live within its means, citing an $11 billion border protection budget blowout under the previous government.

speeches.speaker: Natasha Griggs
speeches.brief: Supported the Customs Amendment Bill, praised the Minister for Immigration and Border Protection's leadership, and recounted Customs and Border Protection interceptions of foreign fishing vessels and drug shipments near Darwin, including a seizure of 1.6 kilograms of heroin, cocaine and methamphetamine.

speeches.speaker: Nola Marino
speeches.brief: Commended the Customs Amendment Bill's technical changes extending Customs powers to non-proclaimed places and domestic legs of international flights, and cited a $630 million investment in security and law enforcement agencies for counterterrorism measures alongside the upcoming Australian Border Force.

speeches.speaker: Barnaby Joyce
speeches.brief: Introduced the Quarantine Charges (Imposition-Customs) Amendment Bill 2014, the second of three charging bills supporting the Biosecurity Bill package, which will impose charges only when they are considered a duty of customs.
